title: TB1-18449
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The adult claimants XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimants), both citizens of El Salvador, and their minor children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor claimants), also citizens of El Salvador, claim refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration And Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 The minor claimants' father was appointed as their designated representative.

The claimants both worked in the financial sector. In XXXX 2011, they were first targeted for extortion by Mara 18 by means of an anonymous note left on their car windshield. They reported the incident to the police and subsequently, the male claimant was physically accosted by gang members seeking to collect monthly payments of several hundred U.S. dollars. When the male claimant failed to comply fully with their demands, they promised to retaliate and demonstrated detailed knowledge of the claimants' movements including those of the minor claimants.

Faced with death threats against them and their daughters, the claimants were extremely frightened. Although they were accepted into the victims and witnesses protection program, no concrete steps were taken by police to ensure their protection while they remained in El Salvador.

Fearing that they would be found and killed by "those people," on November 1, 2011, the claimants flew to New York with the minor claimants. They entered Canada on November 16, 2011 at a land border and made a claim for refugee protection.

After they left El Salvador, the female claimant's parents, the watchman of Urbanization XXXX XXXX where the claimants' home is located and a former colleague of the male claimant reported that unidentified men were making enquiries in an effort to find out his whereabouts.

If removed to El Salvador, the claimants fear for their lives. They fear physical harm, death threats, continued extortion, loss of their livelihood and emotional harm. They also fear for their daughters' safety and are particularly fearful that their daughters could be raped or even killed.
The panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The claimants and the minor claimants have established their respective identities on a balance of probabilities, based on their passports and other identity documents, copies of which are contained in Exhibit 1, and based on the claimants' testimonies.

The claimants' oral testimony was consistent with the allegations contained in their respective Personal Information Form (PIF)2, amendments to PIF narrative of the male claimant3 and their IMM 5611 forms4. They provided supporting documents, including documents proving employment,5 the anonymous note left on their car windshield6, a statement made on XXXX XXXX, 2011 by the male claimant to duty counsel at the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX7, a statement from a physician whom the male claimant consulted on September 30, 20118 about possible injuries from an assault on September 28, 2011, a statement from the female claimant's mother9, a statement from a watchman10, a letter from a former work colleague of the male claimant11, a statement from the children's school12, a written explanation from the Specialized Crime Unit Extortions13, and a case reference card.14

Although they had both held jobs in the financial sector since the 90s, the anonymous note placed on the claimants' car windshield was, according to the claimants, their first personal exposure to gang criminality, in this case, extortion. Their first reaction, as reported in the male claimant's narrative, was that it was a hoax. Upon review of the actual note15, there are quotation marks16 placed around certain words, apparently to draw attention to the euphemistic manner in which they are employed. The quotation marks are out of place given the nature of the document and the author of the document - a gang member using his own vernacular - and raise questions about its genuineness; as such, the panel gives it no weight.

All the other personal documents predating the claimants' departure and which relate to the extortion issue relied on reports of events made to various parties by the male claimant. Therefore although these documents may be authentic, the panel finds that they do not establish the truth of the claimants' allegations on a balance of probabilities.
Furthermore, based on the findings of the panel, the panel affords no weight to the statements of the female claimant's mother, male claimant's work colleague and alleged watchman.
The panel finds that the claimants' allegations and testimony regarding events which they claim to have precipitated their departure from El Salvador were not credible, on a balance of probabilities.

Specifically, the panel finds that the claimants' allegations and testimonies that they were targeted for extortion by Mara 18 beginning in XXXX 2011 or that they were targeted because they both worked in the financial sector and could authorise the disbursement of funds were not established on a balance of probabilities.

Based on the panel's credibility findings, the panel determines that the claimants have not established that there is a serious possibility that they would be persecuted if removed to El Salvador. Moreover, the threats and other criminal acts reported by the claimants do not form a nexus to one of the grounds enumerated in section 96 of the IRPA.

Moreover, as the claimants were not found credible on a balance of probabilities, they have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that if removed to their country of citizenship, they will face a personalized risk to their lives or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

Rather, the risks to life and/or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment that are a source of fear for the claimants, including physical harm, death threats, extortion, loss of livelihood, emotional harm and risk to their daughters of rape or death, are not, with respect to the claimants herein, personalised risks within the meaning of paragraph 97(1) (b) of the IRPA.

As stated by Gleason J. in Portillo v. Canada,17 in an analysis under section of the IRPA, [...] the essential starting point for the required analysis under section 97 of IRPA is to first appropriately determine the nature of the risk faced by the claimant. This requires an assessment of whether the claimant faces an ongoing or future risk (i.e. whether he or she continues to face a "personalized risk"), what the risk is, whether such risk is one of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and the basis for the risk. The next required step in the analysis under section 97 of IRPA, after the risk has been appropriately characterized, is the comparison of the correctly-described risk faced by the claimant to that faced by a significant group in the country to determine whether the risks are of the same nature and degree. If the risk is not the same, then the claimant will be entitled to protection under section 97 of IRPA. Several of the recent decisions of this Court (in the first of the above-described line of cases) adopt this approach.

According to country condition evidence18, there are over 25,000 people who belong to street gangs in El Salvador, and Mara 18 is one of the largest gangs. Moreover, according to the Congressional Research Service Report for Congress entitled "Central America Regional Security Initiative: Background and Policy Issues for Congress"19 (CRS Report); "[...] the gangs have increasingly become involved in extortion, kidnapping, human trafficking, and drug, auto, and weapons smuggling. Gangs have extorted millions of dollars from residents, bus drivers, and businesses in cities throughout the region. Failure to pay often results in harassment or violence. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has also documented increasing numbers of cases of extortion schemes carried out by gangs in El Salvador against Salvadorans in the United States."20 "El Salvador has the highest concentration of gang members, with 323 for every 100,000 citizens..."21 "MS-13 and M-18 began as loosely structured street gangs, but there is evidence that both gangs have expanded geographically, become more organized, and expanded the range of their criminal activities."22

On comparing the risk to the claimants herein to that faced by a significant group in the country, the panel finds it no different in either nature or degree. Members of the community preyed upon by gangs throughout El Salvador face similar risks to those faced by the claimants.

In Wan v M.C.I.,23 Annis J. states that subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii) refers to a risk that must be greater than the risk generally faced by other individuals in the same group as the claimant. Le sous-alinéa 97(1)b)(ii) parle d'un risque qui doit être supérieur à ceux subis généralement par les autres personnes qui font partie du même groupe que le demandeur.24

The panel finds that the claimants' allegations and testimony were not credible, on a balance of probabilities, and they have not demonstrated that the risk to them is greater than that faced by others in their community, and indeed, in communities across the country.

The claimants, therefore, have not established on a balance of probabilities that if removed to El Salvador, they will be subjected to a risk to their lives or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment that is not generally faced by other individuals in and from that country.

Based on the foregoing analysis, the panel finds that the claimants and the minor claimants are neither Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection, and their claims are rejected.
